title: Camp 3 close: your practice
hook: a morning bow, a sitting, a walk, metta, the precepts, a gift, the holy days

segments.voice: Yesterday, kathina, cloth offered for new robes, and your line: the rains end in gifts. What useful thing did you give? Day one hundred fifty-six, the last day of camp three.

On day ninety-seven, camp three began with four short phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Since then you've sat with sixteen steps of the breath, walked a lane of twenty paces, taken the refuges, met the five precepts, given without a receipt, bowed three times, lit a candle, kept the holy days, and learned what a retreat is. That's a lot of practice. Today we gather it into something you can actually keep. Today: your practice.
screen: `DAY 97: FOUR PHRASES.` → `BREATH, WALKING, PRECEPTS, GIVING.` → `NOW, SOMETHING YOU CAN KEEP.`

segments.voice: Camp three was built to add up. By its end, there's a morning, an evening, a week and a year. The morning is the one you built on day one hundred forty-four: a bow, the homage, the breath, a wish of metta, and a dedication of whatever good was done. Ten minutes. The evening can be the metta you learned for sleep, kindness sent out in six directions, or a short sitting of your own, with the hindrances named when they visit. The week holds the rest. A walk that's also a practice, on the lane or on the way to the bus. The five precepts, kept as trainings and taken again whenever one slips. A gift, small and wholehearted, with no receipt. And maybe, now and then, a quiet half-day at home. The year is the holy days: Vesak in May, Asalha Puja in July, the rains retreat and its three-month practice, kathina in the autumn, Magha Puja in February or March. The tradition itself has a pair of words for what we're doing. Pariyatti is learning the teaching: reading, listening, studying. Patipatti is practicing it: sitting, keeping precepts, giving. Camp two was mostly stories, camp three mostly practice. Tomorrow, camp four turns to the text itself: the Dhammapada, a book of the Buddha's sayings in verse, read in order, one piece a day. The practice doesn't stop when the reading starts. Each day's verse will come with a sit and a line to carry, so the words have somewhere to land. You already know how to sit. You know how to bow, walk, give, and begin again.
screen: `A MORNING, AN EVENING.` · `A WEEK: WALK, PRECEPTS, A GIFT.` · `A YEAR: THE HOLY DAYS.` · `STUDY AND PRACTICE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `YOU CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Have something to write with nearby, or just use your mind for now. Sit and breathe. Then sketch your week. Morning: which pieces of the morning practice will you keep? Evening: metta, or a sitting, or both? Somewhere in the week: a walk, a gift, one precept you'll pay attention to. Somewhere in the year: one holy day you'd like to keep. Keep it realistic, not heroic. When the sketch feels right, put it down and just sit with the breath, the way you've done a hundred times now. The bell holds the time.
Patipatti. Practice, the doing of the teaching: a morning, an evening, a week and a year of it, gathered into something you can keep.
Your line: you can do this. Today, write your week down on paper and put it somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning. Day one hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many lay Buddhists keep a simple daily rhythm, such as bowing and chanting at a home shrine in the morning, sitting or metta in the evening, the five precepts through the week, giving to the monastery, and the major holy days through the year.

match.prompt: match each piece of camp three to where it fits.

myth: pariyatti means studying the teaching and patipatti means practicing it
the tradition pairs them: learning and doing.
once the reading of the Dhammapada starts, the sitting stops
each day of camp four keeps a sit and a line to carry.
a good practice plan is the most heroic one you can imagine
keep it realistic: what you can actually keep through busy weeks.

fork.setup: you've written a plan: an hour of sitting every morning. by day three you've missed twice. what fits what camp three taught?
options: give up; it isn't for you.
shrink the plan and begin again.
double it to make up the time.
fork.reveal: the precepts are trainings, taken again and again. a small plan you keep beats a big one you drop.

original.note: Pali: practice, the doing of the teaching, paired with pariyatti, its study.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist practice means long hours of meditation.
what it means: a rhythm of small practices: a morning, an evening, a week and a year.
what a scholar hears: Theravada commentaries speak of pariyatti (study), patipatti (practice) and pativedha (realization) as the three parts of the true teaching.
